id_massacre_rocks.blurb: Massacre Rocks sits in the desert south of American Falls, on the Snake River plain of eastern Idaho. Floodwaters cut the dark basalt into box canyons and alcoves, leaving walls from about 30 to 200 feet. Nearly everything here is bolted sport climbing, on steep to slightly overhanging rock with edges, pockets and the odd crack, and most lines are short. A small number of trad routes and a few boulders round it out. The grades cluster hard in the 5.10 to 5.12 range, with 5.11 the heart of it, a decent run of 5.9 and below, and only a handful of 5.13s. Late fall and early spring are the best windows, sunny winter days can be pleasant, and summer is very hot. Main Wall, Owl Cove Area and All American Area hold the most routes.

co_gunnison.blurb: Gunnison covers the valley around the town and several very different climbing settings. Hartman Rocks, just outside town, offers sculpted granite in an alpine desert, with sport, trad, top-rope and plenty of bouldering. Taylor Canyon is a trad-leaning cliff area, and Spring Creek adds granite walls and towers that are mostly trad. The Black Canyon of the Gunnison is the serious end of the range: steep, narrow granite walls with long, committing multi-pitch trad routes best suited to experienced parties, and its main seasons run from mid-April to early June and mid-September to early November. Across the whole region trad and bouldering lead, followed by sport, with grades mostly from 5.9 to 5.12 and boulder problems from V0 to the mid grades. Cement Creek has some limestone sport climbing.

nl_newfoundland.blurb: Newfoundland is a large island with a lot of sea cliff, especially along its southern and eastern shores, and its climbing is split into four parts: the Avalon Peninsula, the West Coast, the Central and Northeastern Coast, and the South Coast and Burin Peninsula. The Avalon, around St. John's, is by far the most developed and holds most of the climbs, with a strong mix of bouldering, sport and trad. The West Coast adds a notable amount of ice and alpine climbing. Overall bouldering leads, followed by sport and trad, with roped grades mostly from 5.7 to 5.12 and problems from V0 to V6 well represented. Much of the island is still little explored because of its remoteness, so the roadside crags near the capital are the easy starting point.

wi_east_bluff.blurb: East Bluff is the bluff on the east side of Devil's Lake in the Baraboo Range, and it is one of the biggest concentrations of bouldering in the Midwest. The rock is Baraboo quartzite, extremely hard, slick and low on friction, so the climbing is technical and rewards careful footwork. Problems are scattered at lake level, through the talus fields and along the short cliff bands on the upper rim. Bouldering makes up most of the climbs, with some trad and top-rope lines mixed in. The grade spread is wide, from V0 through the mid grades, with a good number of moderates and a thinner tail of hard problems. East Bluff North, East Bluff South and East Bluff South Face are the main sections. Fall is the prime season, while summer is hot and humid.

ca_lost_horse_area.blurb: The Lost Horse Area is a large cluster of walls, buttresses and boulders in Joshua Tree National Park, set in a high valley with big monoliths and formations. The rock is coarse granitic stone with friction slabs, steep faces and splitter cracks, and the elevation keeps it cooler than the lower parts of the park. Trad climbing dominates by a wide margin, with a fair amount of bouldering and top-rope and only a few sport routes. Grades run from 5.4 up to about 5.12, with the bulk between 5.7 and 5.10, so there is plenty for moderate climbers. Some crags sit a short walk from the road, others need a longer trip through a desert wash, and the popular ones such as Hemingway Buttress and Dairy Queen Wall can be busy. Atlantis Area and Lost Horse Wall are also big.

nv_western_nevada.blurb: Western Nevada is a broad region of open sagebrush desert broken by steep, dry mountain ranges, with Reno as its hub and Lake Tahoe close by. Bouldering is the largest share of the climbing, followed by sport and a smaller amount of trad, with a few alpine routes. The Reno Area is mostly boulder problems with many sport routes, Lake Tahoe Area mixes boulders, sport and trad, and Carson City Area adds boulders, sport and trad. Pyramid Lake Area and Lone Mountain lean toward sport. Wild Granites, farther out, holds granite alpine and trad lines. Grades span the full range, from easy boulder problems to hard sport climbs in the 5.12s, with most roped routes in the 5.9 to 5.12 range. Fall is traditionally the best season around Reno and Tahoe.
